body.objective: Students will be able to play basic chords.
successCriteria: I can play C, G, Am and F on guitar or keyboard
I can change chords in time with a steady beat
I can play a strum or comping pattern with a group
body.hook: Thousands of hit songs use the same four chords: I, V, vi and IV. In C major that's C, G, Am and F. Learn those four shapes on guitar or keyboard and you can play along with a surprising amount of music on the radio.

vocabulary.definition: Three or more notes played together.
A three-note chord built from a root, third and fifth.
A chord with a bright sound (root, major third, perfect fifth).
A chord with a darker sound (root, minor third, perfect fifth).
A repeated rhythm for strumming chords.
A diagram showing where to place fingers for a chord.

study.title: Four Chords
study.question: How do musicians use a few chords to play many songs?
study.passage:
Guitar chord shapes (fret numbers, strings low E to high e; x = don't play, 0 = open): C x32010, G 320003, Am x02210, F (easy) xx3211.
Keyboard triads (root position): C = C E G, G = G B D, Am = A C E, F = F A C. Use inversions to move smoothly: G as B D G, F as A C F.
Part 1, Shapes (15 minutes): Learn each chord. Check every string or key rings clearly.
Part 2, Changes (10 minutes): One-minute changes: switch between two chords as many times as you can in one minute. Record your count, then try again.
Part 3, Rhythm (10 minutes): Strum pattern: Down, Down-Up, Up-Down-Up (counted 1, 2 &, & 4 &). Keyboard: play chord on beat 1 and 3, or a broken chord.
Part 4, Ensemble (15 minutes): In groups, play C-G-Am-F, four beats each, with a drum or metronome at 80 bpm. One person counts in "1, 2, 3, 4." Try to stay together and end together.
